questions.q: For a class experiment with electricity, which source does the chapter say is safe to use?
o: Cells, like those used in a wall clock or a TV remote
The socket in the classroom wall
A portable generator kept in the school
A wire taken from an electric pole
questions.a: Cells, like those in a wall clock or a TV remote. The chapter says to use only batteries or cells for experiments; even portable generators can be dangerous.

questions.q: On a cold night a family in Nangal switches on a room heater plugged into the wall. Their electricity comes from the hydroelectric power house at the Bhakra Nangal Dam. Which route of the electricity fits the chapter?
o: Falling water generates it at the power house, it reaches the home through wires, and the heater takes it from the wall socket
Falling water fills cells inside the heater, which the family changes every month
Wind blowing over the dam is carried to the home in batteries
The Sun's energy is captured by the falling water and sent to the heater through the air
questions.a: Falling water generates electricity at the power house, the supply reaches the home through wires, and the heater, plugged into the wall socket, uses it.

questions.q: Match each source (column I) with what it uses to generate electricity (column II). Column I: 1. Windmill  2. Solar panel  3. Hydroelectric power house at a dam  4. A power station that burns fuel. Column II: (p) the Sun's energy  (q) wind energy  (r) falling water  (s) natural gas or coal.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-p, 3-r, 4-s: windmills use wind energy, solar panels capture the Sun's energy, a dam uses falling water and a power station that burns fuel uses natural gas or coal.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A torchlight lamp glows in one position of its switch and does not glow in the other position. Reason (R): A torchlight has two or more electric cells inside it.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. The cells are the source of electricity; it is the position of the switch that decides whether the lamp glows.

questions.q: True or False: Electricity used in our homes can be generated from the force of falling water. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a hydroelectric power house, such as the one at the Bhakra Nangal Dam, uses the force of falling water to generate electricity, which reaches homes through wires
questions.a: True. At a hydroelectric power house, such as the one at the Bhakra Nangal Dam, the force of falling water is used to generate electricity, and this supply reaches homes through wires.

questions.q: (a) Name the three parts you find in a torchlight when you look at it and open it. (b) What happens to the torch lamp when its switch is moved from one position to the other?
s: (a) A lamp, a switch and two or more electric cells
(b) The lamp glows in one position of the switch and does not glow in the other
questions.a: (a) A lamp, a switch, and two or more electric cells inside. (b) The lamp glows in one position of the switch and stops glowing in the other position.

questions.q: Place each device under one of Nihal's headings for the uses of electricity: (a) a scooter, (b) a mixer grinder, (c) a room heater.
s: (a) Scooter: Transportation
(b) Mixer grinder: Cooking
(c) Room heater: Heating and Cooling
questions.a: (a) Transportation. (b) Cooking. (c) Heating and Cooling.

questions.q: The chapter invites you to suggest other ways of grouping the uses of electricity. Asha groups devices by what the electricity is turned into: light, heat or movement. (a) Place a room heater, a fan and an immersion rod under Asha's groups. (b) Using your answer to (a), which one of Nihal's headings is split across two of Asha's groups? (c) Is Nihal's 'Transportation' heading split in the same way? Use a lift and an escalator to decide.
s: (a) Room heater: heat; fan: movement; immersion rod: heat
(b) Heating and Cooling: the room heater and the immersion rod go under heat, but the fan goes under movement
(c) No: a lift and an escalator (like the train, bus, car and scooter) both give movement, so Transportation stays in one of Asha's groups
questions.a: (a) Room heater: heat. Fan: movement. Immersion rod: heat. (b) Heating and Cooling, since its heater and immersion rod give heat while its fan gives movement. (c) No. The lift and the escalator both give movement, as do the other transport devices, so Transportation is not split.

questions.q: A school in Shimla makes a wall chart called 'Electricity in our town'. The town gets electricity from two places: a power house beside a river that flows down from the hills, and solar panels on the roofs of some houses. In one week the school uses 6 tube lights, 4 ceiling fans, 1 water pump and 1 computer, all run on the supply that comes to the school. (a) What does the power house beside the river use to generate electricity, and what do the solar panels capture? (b) Under which of Nihal's headings do the tube lights fall, and under which does the computer? (c) How does electricity from the power house reach the school? (d) How many different headings of Nihal's do the four kinds of devices in the passage cover, and which are they?
s: (a) The force of falling water; the Sun's energy
(b) Tube lights: Lighting; computer: Others
(c) Through wires
(d) 3 headings: Lighting (tube lights), Heating and Cooling (ceiling fans) and Others (water pump and computer)
questions.a: (a) The power house uses the force of falling water; solar panels capture the Sun's energy. (b) Tube lights: Lighting; computer: Others. (c) Through wires. (d) Three headings: Lighting (tube lights), Heating and Cooling (fans), and Others (water pump and computer).

questions.q: For an exhibition on 'Uses of electricity', a Class 7 group in Indore has collected pictures of 8 devices: a television, a radio, an electric kettle, a toaster, a microwave, a refrigerator, a geyser and a mobile phone. They want at least one picture under each of Nihal's 7 headings. (a) Sort the 8 pictures under Nihal's headings. (b) How many headings are covered, and which headings have no picture? (c) Riya says, 'We have 8 pictures and only 7 headings, so every heading must already be covered.' Is she correct? Explain. (d) What is the least number of extra pictures needed? Suggest one from Nihal's lists for each missing heading. (e) The display board has room for only 7 pictures, one under each heading. How many of the 8 pictures must be taken off, and from which headings?
s: (a) Entertainment: television, radio; Cooking: electric kettle, toaster, microwave; Heating and Cooling: refrigerator, geyser; Communication: mobile phone
(b) 4 headings are covered; Lighting, Transportation and Others have no picture

(c) No: several pictures fall under the same heading (3 under Cooking, 2 under Entertainment, 2 under Heating and Cooling), so more pictures than headings does not mean every heading is covered; only 4 are
(d) 3 extra pictures, for example street lights (Lighting), a lift or a train (Transportation) and a water pump or a computer (Others)
(e) 4 pictures are taken off: 2 from Cooking, 1 from Entertainment and 1 from Heating and Cooling, leaving one per covered heading (4 + 3 new = 7)
questions.a: (a) Entertainment: television, radio. Cooking: kettle, toaster, microwave. Heating and Cooling: refrigerator, geyser. Communication: mobile phone. (b) 4 covered; Lighting, Transportation and Others are empty. (c) No. Pictures crowd under the same headings (3 under Cooking, 2 under Entertainment, 2 under Heating and Cooling), so 8 pictures cover only 4 headings. (d) 3, e.g. street lights, a lift or train, and a water pump or computer. (e) Take off 4: two from Cooking, one from Entertainment, one from Heating and Cooling; the 4 kept plus the 3 new make 7, one per heading.

questions.q: Which part of an electric cell is its positive terminal?
o: The small protruding metal cap
The flat metal disc
The outer cover of the cell
The spring of the cell holder
questions.a: The small protruding metal cap is the positive terminal; the flat metal disc is the negative terminal.

questions.q: Two cells are joined to make a battery for a torch so that the lamp glows. Which terminals meet where the two cells touch?
o: The positive terminal of one cell and the negative terminal of the next
The positive terminals of both cells
The negative terminals of both cells
Any two terminals, as the order does not matter
questions.a: The positive terminal of one cell touches the negative terminal of the next; only this order makes the lamp glow.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy. Statement II: The word 'battery' is never used for a single cell. Statement III: In a torch, the cells may be placed in any order and the lamp will still glow. Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
questions.a: Only Statement I is correct. The word battery is also used for a single cell, as in a mobile phone, and the lamp glows only when the cells are placed in the correct order.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The '+' and '-' signs printed inside the battery compartment of a TV remote, where two cells sit side by side, help the user place the cells correctly. Reason (R): In such a compartment a metal strip or thick wire joins the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next, so each cell must face the right way.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because the strip joins the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next, each cell must face a set way, and the printed '+' and '-' signs show that way.

questions.q: (a) What is a battery? (b) Give one reason why many devices use more than one cell.
s: (a) A combination of two or more cells, the positive terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the next
(b) More than one cell gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy
questions.a: (a) A combination of two or more cells in which the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next. (b) It provides energy to the circuit for a longer time and/or more energy.

questions.q: A sealed battery box for a toy train has two wires coming out of it, both the same colour, with no '+' or '-' marks. Ramu has a working LED. (a) Describe how he can use the LED to find which wire comes from the positive terminal of the battery. (b) When the LED glows, how does he know which wire is positive?
s: (a) Join the LED's two wires to the box's two wires; if the LED does not glow, interchange them
(b) When the LED glows, the box wire joined to the LED's longer wire is the positive one
questions.a: (a) Join the two wires of the LED to the two wires of the box; if the LED does not glow, interchange them. (b) An LED glows only when its longer (positive) wire is joined to the positive terminal, so when it glows the box wire on the LED's longer wire is positive.

questions.q: A torch uses three cells placed in a row. (a) What is such a combination of cells called? (b) The metal cap of the first cell faces the second cell. Which terminal of the second cell must it touch for the lamp to glow? (c) Give one benefit of using three cells instead of one.
s: (a) A battery
(b) The negative terminal (flat metal disc) of the second cell
(c) Energy for a longer time and/or more energy
questions.a: (a) A battery. (b) The cap is the positive terminal, so it must touch the negative terminal, the flat metal disc, of the second cell. (c) It gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy.

questions.q: Four torches use the same kind of new cells and the same kind of lamp. Torch P holds 1 cell. Torch Q holds 2 cells, the cap of the first touching the flat disc of the second. Torch R holds 3 cells, each cap touching the flat disc of the next cell. Torch S holds 3 cells placed like R's, except that the middle cell is turned round. (a) Which torches hold a battery in the sense of two or more cells joined positive to negative? (b) Which torch's lamp will not glow, and why? (c) Of the torches whose lamps glow, which does the chapter lead you to expect to give energy to the circuit for the longest time and/or the most energy? Give the reason. (d) Ritu says, 'Torch S has as many cells as torch R, so it must give as much energy as R.' Judge her claim using the data.
s: (a) Q and R (P has a single cell; S's cells are not joined positive to negative)
(b) Torch S: with the middle cell turned round, a cap meets a cap at one joint and a disc meets a disc at the other, so the cells are not in the correct order
(c) Torch R, because connecting more cells correctly gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy, and R has the most cells correctly joined
(d) Not correct: S's lamp does not glow at all; more cells help only when each positive terminal is joined to the next cell's negative terminal
questions.a: (a) Q and R. (b) S: turning the middle cell round makes cap meet cap at one joint and disc meet disc at the other, so the cells are not in the correct order and the lamp stays dark. (c) R, since more cells joined correctly give energy for a longer time and/or more energy. (d) Ritu is wrong: S gives no light at all, because the number of cells helps only when they are joined positive to negative.

questions.q: Ms Rao's class gets 5 torches for a camp. Each torch takes 2 cells in a row, and the class has a box of 12 new cells. After the torches are filled, torches A, B and C glow at once. In torch D the lamp stays dark: the cell next to the lamp has its cap towards the lamp, but the second cell has its flat disc towards the lamp. In torch E the cells are placed correctly and are the same kind that light torch A, but the lamp stays dark with its switch where the student left it. (a) How many cells are left in the box? (b) In torch D, which two terminals meet at the joint, and why does the lamp stay dark? (c) How should torch D be fixed? (d) Rohan says torch E's cells are faulty. Judge his claim using the data and say what to check first.
s: (a) 12 - 5 x 2 = 2 cells left
(b) The flat disc (negative) of the first cell meets the flat disc (negative) of the second; the cells are not joined positive to negative
(c) Turn the second cell round so its cap touches the first cell's disc
(d) Not supported: correctly placed cells of the same kind work in torch A; check the switch position first, since the lamp glows in only one position
questions.a: (a) 2 cells. (b) Negative meets negative (disc against disc), so the cells do not form a battery in the correct order and the lamp stays dark. (c) Turn the second cell round. (d) Rohan's claim is not supported: the cells are correctly placed and the same kind lights torch A, so first slide the switch to its other position, as a torch lamp glows in only one position of the switch.

questions.q: A household has a wall clock that runs on one cylindrical cell, a torch with three cylindrical cells in a row, a TV remote with two cylindrical cells side by side, and a mobile phone with one rechargeable cell. (a) Which of these devices hold a battery in the sense of 'two or more cells joined together'? (b) Cylindrical cells are sold in packs of 4. How many packs must the family buy to refill every device that uses cylindrical cells, and how many cells will be left over? (c) When refilling the torch, which part of each cell must touch the flat disc of the next cell? (d) One evening the family has only 3 new cylindrical cells. Which devices should they refill so that the greatest number of devices works, and why does refilling the torch give fewer? (e) Is it wrong to call the phone's single cell a 'battery'? Explain.
s: (a) The torch and the TV remote
(b) Cylindrical cells needed: 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 (the phone uses a rechargeable cell), so 2 packs (8 cells) with 2 left over
(c) The small protruding metal cap, the positive terminal of the cell
(d) The wall clock (1 cell) and the remote (2 cells): 3 cells make 2 devices work, while the torch alone needs all 3 cells for only 1 device
(e) No; the term battery is also used for a single cell, as for the cell that powers a mobile phone
questions.a: (a) The torch and the remote. (b) 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 cylindrical cells, so 2 packs of 4 (8 cells), leaving 2. (c) The metal cap (positive terminal) of each cell touches the flat disc (negative terminal) of the next. (d) Refill the clock and the remote: the 3 cells then run 2 devices, whereas the torch would use all 3 cells for just 1 device. (e) Not wrong: the term battery is also used for a single cell, such as the one in a mobile phone.

questions.q: What is the thin wire inside the glass bulb of an incandescent lamp, which glows when the lamp is on, called?
o: The filament
The terminal
The insulator
The metal tip
questions.a: The filament: it gets hot and glows to produce light.

questions.q: Sneha notices that one wire of her LED is longer than the other. What does the longer wire tell her?
o: It is the positive terminal of the LED
It is the negative terminal of the LED
It is the filament of the LED
Nothing, as both wires of an LED do the same job
questions.a: The longer wire is the positive terminal of the LED; the shorter wire is the negative terminal.

questions.q: Match each part (column I) with what it is or does (column II). Column I: 1. Filament  2. Metal tip at the centre of the lamp's base  3. Longer wire of an LED  4. Thicker wires inside the glass bulb. Column II: (p) one terminal of an incandescent lamp  (q) gets hot and glows to give light  (r) positive terminal of the LED  (s) support the filament.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-p, 3-r, 4-s: the filament glows, the metal tip is one terminal, the LED's longer wire is positive and the thicker wires hold the filament.

questions.q: Four torch lamps are each joined to a good battery with the switch ON. Lamp 1: incandescent, filament broken. Lamp 2: LED, longer wire joined to the battery's negative terminal. Lamp 3: incandescent, filament whole, metal tip joined to the negative terminal and metal case to the positive. Lamp 4: LED, longer wire joined to the positive terminal and shorter wire to the negative. Which lamps glow?
o: Lamps 3 and 4 only
Lamp 4 only
Lamps 2, 3 and 4
Lamps 1 and 3 only
questions.a: Lamps 3 and 4 only. A broken filament stops the current (lamp 1), an LED passes current only when its longer wire is on the positive (lamp 2 fails, lamp 4 glows), and an incandescent lamp glows whichever terminal goes to the positive (lamp 3).

questions.q: True or False: An LED gives light because a thin filament inside it gets hot and glows. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: an LED has no filament; it is the incandescent lamp whose filament gets hot and glows
questions.a: False. LEDs do not have filaments. It is an incandescent lamp whose thin filament gets hot and glows to give light.

questions.q: Lata has two torch lamps. In lamp X she can see a thin wire inside the glass bulb. Lamp Y has no thin wire inside and has two wires of unequal length. (a) Name the type of each lamp. (b) For which lamp does it matter which wire is joined to the battery's positive terminal, and why?
s: (a) X: incandescent lamp; Y: LED
(b) Lamp Y, the LED, because current passes through an LED in one direction only; its longer wire must go to the positive terminal
questions.a: (a) X is an incandescent lamp (it has a filament); Y is an LED. (b) It matters for the LED: current passes through it in one direction only, so its longer wire must be joined to the battery's positive terminal. For the incandescent lamp either way works.

questions.q: (a) Which part of an incandescent lamp glows when the lamp is switched on? (b) What happens to this part when current passes through it? (c) What do we say about a lamp that does not glow because this part is broken?
s: (a) The filament
(b) It gets hot and glows to produce light
(c) The lamp has 'fused'
questions.a: (a) The filament. (b) It gets hot and glows, producing light. (c) We say the lamp has fused; the broken filament stops the flow of current.

questions.q: Tara's battery has two wires: wire F is joined to its positive terminal and wire S to its negative terminal. She has a red LED with legs 2.0 cm and 1.6 cm long, and a green LED with legs 1.7 cm and 2.2 cm long. Each time she joins the first leg named to wire F and the second leg named to wire S. (a) Does the red LED glow? Give the reason. (b) Does the green LED glow? Give the reason. (c) Her friend says, 'The green LED is faulty, because green LEDs do not work with this battery.' Judge the claim and say what Tara should do.
s: (a) Yes: its longer (2.0 cm) leg, the positive terminal, is on the positive wire F
(b) No: its longer (2.2 cm) leg is on the negative wire S, and current passes through an LED in one direction only
(c) Not supported: the colour does not matter; the green LED is joined the wrong way round, so she should interchange its legs (2.2 cm leg to F) and it will glow
questions.a: (a) Yes, because the longer 2.0 cm leg (positive terminal) is joined to the positive wire F. (b) No. Its longer 2.2 cm leg went to the negative wire S, and current passes through an LED in one direction only. (c) The claim is not supported: LEDs of any colour work this way; the green one is simply reversed. She should interchange its legs so the 2.2 cm leg goes to F.

questions.q: For a science model, Uday draws a large copy of an incandescent torch lamp and labels it. P: a thin wire in the middle of the glass bulb. Q and R: two thicker wires that hold P. Q goes to the metal tip at the centre of the base, and R also goes to the metal tip. T: a small metal bead fixed between Q and R to hold them steady. (a) Which labelled part is the filament? (b) Which label is wrong about where its wire goes, and what should it say? (c) With that label corrected, what are the two terminals of the lamp? (d) His teacher says T must be made of an insulator, not metal. Give the reason, using what the chapter says about the thick wires and about insulators.
s: (a) P
(b) R is wrong: one thick wire goes to the metal tip, so R must go to the metal case at the lamp's base
(c) The metal tip at the centre of the base and the metal case at the base

(d) The two thick wires must be fixed so that they do not touch each other; a metal bead would join them because metal is a conductor, while an insulator does not let current pass, so it can hold them apart
questions.a: (a) P, the thin wire that glows. (b) R: it should go to the metal case at the base, since Q already goes to the metal tip. (c) The metal tip and the metal case. (d) The thick wires are fixed so that they do not touch each other. A metal bead is a conductor and would join them; an insulator does not let current pass, so it can support them while keeping them apart.

questions.q: Kiran compares two torches. The old torch has a lamp with a thin wire inside its glass bulb. The new torch has a lamp made of five small LEDs, two round and three square, and Kiran finds that this lamp cannot be taken out because it is fixed in the torch. (a) What type of lamp does the old torch have? (b) What kind of lamp do many torches in use today have, like Kiran's new torch? (c) Kiran's friend says a lamp that cannot be taken out of a torch must be broken. Is this right? (d) Kiran's sister says a torch lamp cannot have LEDs of different shapes. Is she right, according to the chapter? (e) Each LED in the new lamp has two wires. How many wires come out of the five LEDs in all, and how many of them are positive terminals?
s: (a) An incandescent lamp
(b) A Light Emitting Diode (LED) lamp
(c) No; some torches have a different kind of lamp that is fixed in the torch and cannot be taken out
(d) No; a torch may use one or more LEDs, sometimes of different shapes, in its lamp
(e) 5 x 2 = 10 wires, of which 5 (the longer wire of each LED) are positive terminals
questions.a: (a) An incandescent lamp, as it has a thin wire (filament) inside. (b) An LED lamp. (c) No: the chapter mentions torches with a different kind of lamp that is fixed in the torch and cannot be taken out. (d) She is not right: a torch may use one or more LEDs, sometimes of different shapes. (e) 10 wires; 5 of them, the longer wire of each LED, are positive terminals.

questions.q: When the switch in a circuit is in the OFF position, what is the state of the circuit?
o: Open: there is a gap, so no current flows
Closed: the path is complete, so current flows
Open, but current still flows through the switch
Closed, but the lamp does not glow
questions.a: The circuit is open: the switch leaves a gap, so current cannot flow and the lamp does not glow.

questions.q: In a model house a battery sits in the kitchen, and a single loop of wire runs from it to a lamp in the bedroom and back. Arjun wants one switch beside the front door to turn the lamp on and off. The door is on the wire that runs back from the lamp to the battery's negative terminal. Which statement is correct?
o: The switch will work there, because a switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit
The switch must sit beside the battery's positive terminal, where the current starts
The switch must sit right beside the lamp, or it cannot control the lamp
The switch will not work there, because no current flows on the wire to the negative terminal
questions.a: The switch will work beside the door: a switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, and opening it anywhere in the single loop breaks the path.

questions.q: Read the statements about a circuit with a cell, a lamp and a switch. Statement I: A switch can be placed anywhere in the circuit. Statement II: In the ON position the switch leaves a gap in the circuit. Statement III: The lamp glows only when current passes through the circuit. Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. In the ON position the switch closes the gap and completes the path; the gap is there in the OFF position.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The switches used for lights at home turn a lamp on and off in the same way as a safety-pin switch does. Reason (R): A switch is a simple device that either completes or breaks a circuit.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: home switches, though designed differently, also work by completing or breaking the circuit.

questions.q: (a) What is an electrical circuit? (b) In which direction is the electric current taken to flow in a circuit?
s: (a) A complete path for electric current, formed when the two terminals of the lamp are connected to the two terminals of the cell
(b) From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell
questions.a: (a) A setup that provides a complete path for current, with one terminal of the lamp joined to one terminal of the cell and the other to the other. (b) From the positive to the negative terminal of the cell.

questions.q: True or False: In a loop of a two-cell battery, a switch and an LED that is glowing, turning the switch to OFF and turning the battery round both stop the LED glowing for the same reason. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False

Reason: the OFF switch leaves a gap, so the circuit is open; turning the battery round keeps the path complete, but current would now have to pass through the LED in the wrong direction, and it passes in one direction only
questions.a: False. With the switch OFF there is a gap, so the circuit is open and no current flows. With the battery turned round the path is still complete, but the LED's longer wire is now on the negative side, and current can pass through an LED in one direction only, so it stays dark for a different reason.

questions.q: Two incandescent lamps L1 and L2 and one switch are joined in a single loop with a two-cell battery, so that the current must pass through L1 and then L2. (a) With the switch ON and both lamps good, do both lamps glow? (b) The filament of L1 breaks. Does L2 glow? (c) Give the reason for your answer to (b).
s: (a) Yes, both glow, because the path is complete
(b) No, L2 does not glow
(c) The broken filament makes a gap in the only path, so no current flows through L2 either
questions.a: (a) Yes, the circuit is complete. (b) No. (c) A broken filament stops the flow of current; since L1 is on the only path, the circuit becomes open and no current reaches L2.

questions.q: A model house has three rooms, each with its own loop of one cell, one switch and one incandescent lamp. Room 1: switch ON, filament whole. Room 2: switch ON, filament broken. Room 3: switch OFF, filament whole. (a) In which rooms does the lamp glow? (b) Why is the circuit open in room 2 and in room 3? (c) Ranjan says, 'Rooms 2 and 3 have the same fault, so the same repair will fix both.' Is he correct?
s: (a) Only room 1
(b) Room 2: the broken filament makes a gap inside the lamp; room 3: the switch in the OFF position leaves a gap
(c) No, he is not correct: both circuits are open, but the gaps differ (a broken filament in room 2, an OFF switch in room 3), so room 2 needs a new lamp and room 3 only needs the switch turned ON
questions.a: (a) Room 1 only. (b) In room 2 the broken filament breaks the path inside the lamp; in room 3 the OFF switch leaves a gap. (c) No, he is not correct. Both circuits are open, but the gaps are different, so the repairs differ: replace the fused lamp in room 2, turn the switch ON in room 3.

questions.q: Neeta has a cell in a cell holder, a torch lamp in a lamp holder, a home-made safety-pin switch and three wires. She wants the switch to turn the lamp on and off. (a) How should she prepare the ends of each wire? (b) Describe how she should join the parts. (c) What does she see when the safety pin touches both drawing pins, and why? (d) In which direction does the current flow in her circuit?
s: (a) Remove about 1 cm of the plastic covering from both ends of each wire to expose the metal
(b) Join the cell holder, the switch and the lamp holder in one loop, each wire joining the terminal of one part to the next
(c) The lamp glows: the pin closes the gap, the circuit is closed and current flows
(d) From the positive terminal of the cell, round the loop, to the negative terminal
questions.a: (a) Strip about 1 cm of plastic from both ends. (b) One loop: cell holder to switch, switch to lamp holder, lamp holder back to the cell holder. (c) The lamp glows, because the safety pin completes the path (ON, closed circuit). (d) From the cell's positive terminal to its negative terminal.

questions.q: For a science fair in Bhopal, Tanvi builds a door alarm from a two-cell battery, an LED, wires and a safety-pin switch fixed to the door frame. The battery's positive terminal is joined to the LED's longer wire, the LED's shorter wire to the first drawing pin, and the second drawing pin to the battery's negative terminal. When the door is shut it pushes the safety pin away from the second drawing pin; when the door opens, a rubber band pulls the pin onto the second drawing pin. (a) With the door shut, is the circuit open or closed, and does the LED glow? (b) When the door opens, trace the path of the current from the battery round the loop. (c) Tanvi wants to move the switch so that it sits between the battery's positive terminal and the LED. Will the alarm still work? Give the reason. (d) Her friend proposes Design 2, in which the pin rests on the second drawing pin while the door is shut and is pulled away when it opens. Which design makes the LED glow only when someone opens the door? Justify.
s: (a) Open: the pin leaves a gap, so no current flows and the LED does not glow

(b) From the positive terminal to the LED's longer wire, through the LED, out of its shorter wire to the first drawing pin, through the safety pin to the second drawing pin, and back to the negative terminal
(c) Yes; a switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, and the LED's longer wire still goes to the positive side

(d) Tanvi's design: opening the door closes the gap and the LED glows; in Design 2 the circuit is closed while the door is shut (LED glows) and opened when the door opens (LED goes dark), the opposite of an alarm
questions.a: (a) Open; the gap stops the current, so the LED is dark. (b) Positive terminal, LED (longer wire in, shorter wire out), first drawing pin, safety pin, second drawing pin, negative terminal. (c) Yes, because a switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit; it still opens or closes the one path, and the LED still faces the right way. (d) Tanvi's own design. Opening the door closes her switch, so the LED glows only then; Design 2 keeps the LED glowing while the door is shut and turns it off when the door opens.

questions.q: In the circuit symbol of an electric cell, which part stands for the positive terminal?
o: The longer line
The shorter line
The gap between the two lines
The wire drawn to the right of the cell
questions.a: The longer line stands for the positive terminal; the shorter line stands for the negative terminal.

questions.q: A circuit diagram shows one loop: a battery, a switch symbol drawn with a gap, and an LED symbol whose triangle points round the loop from the battery's long-line end towards its short-line end. What does this diagram tell you?
o: The LED is joined the right way round but will not glow until the switch is closed
The LED is glowing now
The LED is joined the wrong way round
The diagram cannot show whether the switch is ON or OFF
questions.a: The LED is joined the right way round (its triangle points from the positive to the negative side, the way current flows) but will not glow until the switch is closed, because a switch drawn with a gap is in the OFF position.

questions.q: Match each feature of a circuit symbol (column I) with what it shows (column II). Column I: 1. Long line in the cell symbol  2. Triangle in the LED symbol  3. Two arrows in the LED symbol  4. Switch symbol drawn with a gap. Column II: (p) the LED gives out light  (q) the positive terminal  (r) the direction in which current can flow  (s) the switch is OFF.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-r, 3-p, 4-s: the long line is positive, the triangle points the way current can flow, the arrows show the LED emits light, and a gap means OFF.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A neat drawing that shows the real shapes of a cell, a torch lamp and a safety-pin switch joined by wires is a circuit diagram. Reason (R): A circuit diagram is a representation of an electrical circuit using symbols.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false but R is true: a circuit diagram uses symbols, such as the long and short lines for a cell, not drawings of the real shapes of the parts.

questions.q: (a) What is a circuit diagram? (b) Give one advantage of using symbols for electrical components.
s: (a) A representation of an electrical circuit using symbols
(b) It makes circuits easier to draw and understand (and standard symbols are understood across the world)
questions.a: (a) A representation of an electrical circuit using symbols. (b) Symbols make a circuit easier to draw and to understand.

questions.q: A simple torch has two cells, a switch and an incandescent lamp. (a) Name the symbols you would use to draw its circuit diagram. (b) How must these symbols be joined in the diagram?
s: (a) A battery symbol (two cell symbols), a switch symbol and an electric lamp symbol, with wires drawn as lines
(b) All in one closed loop, the wire lines joining battery, switch and lamp end to end
questions.a: (a) The battery (two cells), switch and electric lamp symbols, with lines for wires. (b) Joined in one complete loop: battery to switch, switch to lamp, lamp back to the battery.

questions.q: Name the component shown by each symbol described below: (a) one long line and one short line side by side; (b) a triangle pointing in one direction with two small arrows beside it; (c) two or more pairs of long and short lines joined in a row.
s: (a) An electric cell
(b) A light emitting diode (LED)
(c) A battery
questions.a: (a) An electric cell. (b) An LED. (c) A battery.

questions.q: Arif has a correct circuit diagram of a torch with an incandescent lamp. He says, 'If I replace the lamp symbol with an LED symbol, I must also check which way the triangle points.' Is he correct? Explain using what the chapter says about LEDs and their symbol.
s: Verdict: Yes, he is correct
Current passes through an LED in one direction only, while an incandescent lamp glows either way
The triangle shows the direction in which current can flow, so it must point from the battery's positive (long line) side towards its negative side
questions.a: Yes. An LED lets current pass in one direction only, and in its symbol the triangle points in that direction, so the triangle must point the way current flows, from the positive side to the negative side. The lamp symbol had no such direction because an incandescent lamp works either way.

questions.q: A circuit diagram shows one loop: a battery drawn as two cell symbols, a switch symbol S1, an electric lamp symbol and a second switch symbol S2. S1 is drawn with a gap and S2 is drawn closed. (a) In which position, ON or OFF, is each switch in the real circuit? (b) Does the lamp glow as drawn? Give the reason. (c) Jaya says, 'Draw the lamp symbol the other way round and the lamp will glow.' Is she correct? Give the reason. (d) What is the one change to the drawing that shows the lamp glowing, and after that change, what change to S2 alone would show the lamp off again?
s: (a) S1 is OFF and S2 is ON
(b) No: the gap at S1 leaves the circuit open, so no current flows, even though S2 is ON
(c) No: an electric (incandescent) lamp glows whichever way it is joined; the fault is the open switch S1, not the lamp
(d) Draw S1 closed (ON); then drawing S2 with a gap (OFF) would show the lamp off again, since the loop has only one path
questions.a: (a) S1 OFF, S2 ON. (b) No. The gap at S1 makes the circuit open, so no current flows through the lamp. (c) No: an incandescent lamp works either way round; the gap at S1 is the reason it is dark. (d) Redraw S1 closed; then redrawing S2 with a gap would open the single loop again and show the lamp off.

questions.q: Mira turns a picture of a circuit into a circuit diagram. The picture shows two cells in a holder, wires, a safety-pin switch whose pin is not touching the second drawing pin, and an incandescent torch lamp, all in one loop. (a) Which symbol should she draw for the two cells? (b) Which switch symbol should she draw, and why? (c) Does it matter which way round she draws the lamp symbol? Give a reason. (d) Will the lamp glow in the circuit as pictured? (e) Why is her diagram easier to share with a student in another country than the picture?
s: (a) The battery symbol
(b) The switch in the OFF position, because the pin does not touch the second drawing pin and leaves a gap
(c) No; an incandescent lamp glows whichever way it is joined
(d) No, the circuit is open
(e) Standard symbols, made by organisations such as the IEC, are understood by people in different countries
questions.a: (a) The battery symbol. (b) Switch OFF, as the pin leaves a gap. (c) No, an incandescent lamp works either way round. (d) No, the gap makes the circuit open. (e) It uses standard symbols, set by bodies such as the IEC, ANSI and IEEE, so people in different countries understand it easily.

questions.q: Hina touches the free ends of a working conduction tester to the two ends of each object. For which object will the lamp glow?
o: A strip of aluminium foil
A rubber eraser
A wooden stick
A plastic scale
questions.a: The aluminium foil, because it is a metal and metals are conductors of electricity; rubber, wood and plastic are insulators.

questions.q: Which of these devices usually runs on Direct Current (DC) from a cell?
o: A hearing aid
A geyser
A refrigerator
An air conditioner
questions.a: A hearing aid: it runs on a button cell, and electricity from cells and batteries is Direct Current; the geyser, refrigerator and air conditioner are larger appliances that run on Alternating Current from the wall socket.

questions.q: Ira makes a new conduction tester and wants the part of each wire she holds to be safe while the circuit still works. Which design uses both kinds of material correctly?
o: A copper wire inside, covered with plastic or rubber where she holds it
A plastic wire inside, covered with copper on the outside
A rubber wire inside, covered with aluminium foil
A bare copper wire with no covering at all
questions.a: A copper wire inside with a plastic or rubber covering: the copper conductor carries the current, and the insulator covering protects her from electric shock.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: Our body is a conductor of electricity. Statement II: Plastic, rubber and ceramics are used to cover wires, plug tops and switches. Statement III: Silver, copper and gold are the best electrical conductors. Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
questions.a: All three statements are correct, as the chapter states each of them.

questions.q: True or False: We should never touch a switch or a plug with wet hands. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: our body is a conductor of electricity, and current passing through it can cause severe injury or even death
questions.a: True. Our body is a conductor of electricity; electric current passing through it may cause severe injury or even death, so switches and plugs must never be touched with wet hands.

questions.q: (a) What are insulators? (b) Name two materials used as insulators to cover electric wires.
s: (a) Materials through which electric current cannot pass (poor conductors of electricity)
(b) Any two of: plastic, rubber, ceramics
questions.a: (a) Materials through which current cannot pass; also called poor conductors of electricity. (b) Any two of plastic, rubber and ceramics.

questions.q: Cells come in different types: cylindrical, button and rechargeable. Name the type usually used in (a) a hearing aid, (b) a laptop, (c) a wall clock.
s: (a) Button cell
(b) Rechargeable battery
(c) Cylindrical cell
questions.a: (a) A button cell. (b) A rechargeable battery. (c) A cylindrical cell.

questions.q: Rani tested three objects with a conduction tester. The lamp glowed for two of them and stayed dark for the third. Suggest three objects, from those used in the chapter's activity, that would give exactly this result. Name the material of each and say which one is the insulator.
s: Two objects made of metal, for example a key and a sewing needle, with their material named
One object made of an insulating material, for example a candle (wax), a wooden stick or a rubber eraser, with its material named
The lamp glows for the two metal (conductor) objects; the third is the insulator
questions.a: For example: a key (metal) and a sewing needle (metal), on which the lamp glows because metals are conductors, and a candle (wax), which is the insulator. Any two metal objects and one of wax, wood, rubber, plastic or paper is acceptable.

questions.q: Zoya visits an electrical shop for a project. She lists a wristwatch, a hearing aid, a toy car, a TV remote, a laptop, an electric scooter and, on the shop wall, a refrigerator plugged into a socket. (a) Name the type of cell the shop would sell for (i) the wristwatch, (ii) the TV remote, (iii) a mobile phone. (b) What type of current do the cells and batteries give, and what type does the refrigerator get from the wall socket? (c) Her brother says, 'The electric scooter is a big machine, so its battery must give Alternating Current like the wall socket.' Is he correct? Explain. (d) Zoya says the chapter's line 'electricity from batteries usually powers small devices' is wrong because of the scooter. Judge her claim.
s: (a) (i) Button cell, (ii) cylindrical battery, (iii) rechargeable battery
(b) Cells and batteries give Direct Current (DC); the wall socket gives Alternating Current (AC)
(c) No; the scooter runs on a battery (rechargeable batteries are used for electric vehicles), and electricity from a battery is Direct Current

(d) Not wrong: the line says 'usually', so most battery devices are small; the chapter itself lists electric vehicles among the uses of rechargeable batteries, so the scooter is an exception it allows for
questions.a: (a) (i) Button cell (watch), (ii) cylindrical battery (remote), (iii) rechargeable battery (mobile phone). (b) Batteries give DC; the wall socket gives AC. (c) No. Electric vehicles run on rechargeable batteries, and electricity from batteries is DC, whatever the size of the machine. (d) Her claim does not hold: 'usually' means most battery devices are small, not all, and the chapter itself names electric vehicles as users of rechargeable batteries.

questions.q: Rohit tests five objects with a conduction tester and records: metal key, lamp glows; rubber eraser, lamp dark; electric plug (wire ends touched to two points on its plastic top), lamp dark; wooden stick, lamp dark; electric wire (wire ends touched to two points on its plastic covering), lamp dark. He then sorts them into the chapter's three groups: 'conductor only': key; 'insulator only': eraser, plug, stick and wire; 'made of both': none. (a) Which of his placings are correct? Give the reasons. (b) What is wrong with placing the plug under 'insulator only'? (c) What is wrong with placing the wire under 'insulator only'? (d) Describe one test with the tester that would show the wire contains a conductor. (e) After correcting his list, how many objects are in each of the three groups?
s: (a) Key under conductor only (metal is a conductor); eraser and stick under insulator only (rubber and wood are insulators)
(b) A plug's connectors are made of conductors and only its top is an insulator, so it is made of both; he tested only the top
(c) A wire has metal inside, a conductor, with a plastic insulator covering, so it is made of both
(d) Remove about 1 cm of the covering at both ends and touch the tester's free ends to the bare metal; the lamp glows
(e) Conductor only: 1 (key); insulator only: 2 (eraser, stick); made of both: 2 (plug, wire)
questions.a: (a) The key (metal, conductor only), the eraser (rubber) and the stick (wood), both insulator only, are correct. (b) The plug's connectors are conductors and only its top is an insulator, so it belongs under 'made of both'; touching only the plastic top could not show the connectors. (c) The wire's metal inside is a conductor and its plastic covering an insulator, so it too is made of both. (d) Strip about 1 cm of covering from both ends and touch the tester to the bare metal: the lamp glows. (e) 1 conductor only, 2 insulator only, 2 made of both.
